# Research: Preset 01 — Cloister Organum  
## History / Primary-Source Report

## Summary

A historically coherent preset can reference the **late-twelfth- and early-thirteenth-century Notre-Dame organum tradition shared by the repertories associated with Léonin and Pérotin**: liturgical chant retained as a structural tenor, expanded by one or more newly composed voices, with perfect consonances serving as important structural sonorities. It should not blend Léonin’s predominantly two-voice, alternately florid and discant practice with Pérotin’s rhythmically coordinated three- and four-voice writing into a generic “medieval” texture.

The catalog phrase **“open fourths, fifths, and octaves around a chant line” is only partly defensible**. Fourths, fifths, and octaves belong to the documented consonance vocabulary, but Notre-Dame organum is not simply constant parallel interval doubling; the chant normally occupies the lowest tenor, upper voices are melodically and rhythmically active, and non-perfect vertical intervals occur between structural consonances. A reactive MIDI preset may honestly claim a **bounded modern evocation of chant-supported Notre-Dame organum**, not reconstruction, authentic performance, or imitation of either named composer.

---

## 1. Scope and corpus

### 1.1 Referenced period

This report scopes the preset to the **Notre-Dame polyphonic repertory of approximately the later twelfth through early thirteenth centuries**, as transmitted principally in thirteenth-century manuscripts and described retrospectively by the theorist conventionally called Anonymous IV.

The preset does **not** represent:

- ninth-century parallel organum as described in the *Musica enchiriadis* tradition;
- all medieval sacred polyphony;
- later thirteenth-century motets derived from Notre-Dame clausulae;
- conductus as an interchangeable substitute for chant-based organum;
- modern “monastic,” drone, or cinematic-medieval ambience.

### 1.2 Principal musical witnesses

The most substantial consulted witness is Florence, Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana, **MS Pluteus 29.1**, conventionally **F**. DIAMM describes it as containing 863 compositions and exposes manuscript images through IIIF. Its organization preserves distinct four-, three-, and two-voice repertory groups rather than one homogeneous style. [DIAMM manuscript record](https://www.diamm.ac.uk/sources/924/)

Particularly relevant folios are:

| Repertory item | Florence F location | Evidentiary significance |
|---|---:|---|
| *Viderunt omnes / Notum fecit*, four voices | ff. 1–4 | Monumental four-voice organum traditionally associated with Pérotin |
| *Sederunt principes / Adiuva me*, four voices | ff. 4–7v | Second named Pérotin quadruplum in Anonymous IV’s report |
| *Viderunt omnes / Notum fecit*, two voices | ff. 99–100v | Demonstrates a separate duplum tradition on the same chant |
| *Sederunt / Adiuva me*, two voices | ff. 101–102 | Two-voice counterpart to the four-voice repertory |
| *Alleluia Pascha nostrum*, two voices | ff. 109–109v | Representative chant-based organum duplum |
| Numerous short two-voice clausulae | approximately ff. 147–184v | Evidence for replacement clausulae and repertorial revision |

These locations are taken from the DIAMM contents record, which importantly catalogs the manuscript pieces as **anonymous**. The composer names come from treatise testimony and later scholarly attribution, not from signatures in F. [DIAMM manuscript contents](https://www.diamm.ac.uk/sources/924/)

Other principal witnesses include:

- Wolfenbüttel, Herzog August Bibliothek, **Cod. Guelf. 628 Helmst. (W1)**, a major *Magnus liber organi* source. [DIAMM W1 record](https://www.diamm.ac.uk/sources/870/)
- Wolfenbüttel, Herzog August Bibliothek, **Cod. Guelf. 1099 Helmst. (W2)**, another major thirteenth-century Notre-Dame source. [DIAMM W2 record](https://www.diamm.ac.uk/sources/854/)
- The modern critical *Magnus Liber Organi* series and Mark Everist’s annotated transcriptions of F. Everist cautions that these transcriptions do not replace the full critical edition but are intended as scholarly and performing resources. [DIAMM transcription project](https://www.diamm.ac.uk/resources/music-editions/organa-and-clausulae-ms-i-fl-pluteus-291/)

### 1.3 Treatise corpus

The central near-contemporary narrative source is **Anonymous IV, *De mensuris et discantu***, probably written several decades after the principal activity it describes. The standard editions/translations include:

- Fritz Reckow, *Der Musiktraktat des Anonymus 4*, 2 vols., Beihefte zum Archiv für Musikwissenschaft 4–5 (Wiesbaden: Franz Steiner, 1967), especially vol. 1, pp. 45–46.
- Jeremy Yudkin, *The Music Treatise of Anonymous IV: A New Translation* (Neuhausen-Stuttgart: Hänssler-Verlag, 1985). [Internet Archive catalog](https://archive.org/details/musictreatiseofa0000unse)
- Anonymous IV, Latin/French working edition, with discussion of its description of the *Magnus liber organi* and its reported succession of Parisian masters. [HAL edition](https://shs.hal.science/halshs-04198547v1/file/Anonyme%20IV%20(latin:Fran%C3%A7ais).pdf)

For compositional vocabulary and rhythm, this report also considers the Notre-Dame theoretical tradition represented by *De mensurabili musica*, conventionally attributed to Johannes de Garlandia:

- Erich Reimer, ed., *Johannes de Garlandia: De mensurabili musica*, 2 vols., Beihefte zum Archiv für Musikwissenschaft 10–11 (Wiesbaden: Franz Steiner, 1972). [Critical-edition scan, vol. 1](https://www.examenapium.it/meri/pdf/Reimer1.pdf)
- Stanley H. Birnbaum, trans., *Concerning Measured Music: De mensurabili musica* (Colorado Springs: Colorado College Music Press, 1978). [Internet Archive catalog](https://archive.org/details/concerningmeasur0000joha)

### 1.4 Attribution limit

No surviving autograph by Léonin or Pérotin was identified. F, W1, and W2 are later repertory witnesses, and their musical contents are mostly anonymous. The correct formulation is therefore:

> “Repertory associated by Anonymous IV and subsequent scholarship with Léonin and Pérotin,”

not:

> “scores demonstrably written and copied by Léonin and Pérotin.”

---

## 2. Historical and aesthetic context

### 2.1 Liturgical enlargement, not free-standing harmonic composition

Anonymous IV reports that a certain **Magister Leoninus** was an excellent maker of organa and made a great book of organum from the Gradual and Antiphoner **“for the amplification of the divine service”**—*pro servitio divino multiplicando*. The report presents polyphony as an enlargement of pre-existing liturgical chant, not as a progression of autonomous chords.

The chant therefore has three simultaneous roles:

1. inherited liturgical material;
2. formal map determining which textual and melodic portions receive polyphony;
3. structural tenor beneath newly composed voice or voices.

This is the strongest historical basis for the preset’s chant-line concept.

Primary passage: Anonymous IV, *De mensuris et discantu*, in Reckow, vol. 1, pp. 45–46; discussed and translated in Edward H. Roesner, “Who ‘Made’ the *Magnus Liber*?”, *Early Music History* 20 (2001), opening discussion and note 1. [Article record](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0261127901001061) · [Accessible article PDF](http://www.examenapium.it/cs/biblio/Roesner2001.pdf)

### 2.2 Selective festal practice

The repertory is not evidence that every chant or every service was continuously polyphonic. The great organa elaborate selected responsorial chants, especially Graduals, Alleluias, and Office responsories appropriate to important feasts. Guillaume Gross characterizes the tripla and quadrupla as virtuosic pieces intended for celebration of the **greatest feasts** in the new cathedral. [Gross, “Organum at Notre-Dame,” abstract and bibliographic record](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0961137106000349)

The alternation of polyphonic and unembellished chant portions matters aesthetically. Notre-Dame organum creates expansion and contrast within a liturgical framework; it is not an uninterrupted “open medieval chord pad.”

### 2.3 Cathedral and institutional context

“Cloister” is evocative product language, but the referenced repertory is specifically associated with an **urban cathedral and its clerical and educational institutions**, not securely with secluded monastic practice. “Cloister Organum” should therefore remain an image-title, not historical metadata.

Similarly, “Notre-Dame School” is a useful modern category but can imply a firmer institution, canon, and composer succession than the evidence warrants. The repertory circulated beyond Paris, and its manuscripts were copied later and in several locations.

### 2.4 Notational and rhythmic problem

Notre-Dame notation records pitch and patterned rhythm with greater specificity in discant passages than in sustained-tenor organum purum, whose rhythmic realization remains disputed. Modern equal-tempered MIDI necessarily imposes exact onset, duration, pitch, and voice-assignment decisions that the sources and treatises do not always determine uniquely.

That limitation prevents the preset from claiming historically authentic timing or performance practice.

---

## 3. Career and repertory evolution

Biographical “career” reconstruction is unusually hazardous here. The report therefore distinguishes **treatise narrative**, **repertory layers**, and **secure biography**.

### 3.1 Léonin-associated layer

Anonymous IV calls Léonin an excellent **organista** and associates him with the making of a *magnus liber organi* based on Gradual and Antiphonal chants. The principal stylistic category linked by scholarship to this layer is **organum duplum**:

- a chant-bearing tenor;
- one added voice, the duplum;
- sustained-tenor **organum purum** where a chant note may be greatly prolonged beneath a florid upper melody;
- measured **discant** where tenor and duplum participate in patterned rhythm;
- alternation governed partly by the chant’s syllabic and melismatic construction.

Asher Yampolsky’s score-based dissertation describes organum duplum as the preponderant Notre-Dame organum type and defines its main texture as a prolonged chant tenor under a newly composed upper line. His analysis also supports hearing organum purum as both modal and “dronal,” rather than merely as arbitrary consonant interval doubling. [Yampolsky, *Melodic Mode in Notre Dame Organum Duplum*, abstract](https://eprints.soton.ac.uk/482281/)

**Biographical confidence:** low to medium. Anonymous IV’s testimony is late; identification of the musician with a documented Parisian cleric or poet named Leonius remains debated.

### 3.2 Pérotin-associated revision and enlargement

Anonymous IV reports that **Perotinus Magnus**, praised as an excellent **discantor**, abbreviated or edited the book and made better replacement clausulae or *puncta*. He specifically names:

- the four-voice *Viderunt omnes*;
- the four-voice *Sederunt principes*;
- three-voice pieces including *Alleluia Posui adiutorium* and *Nativitas*.

The F manuscript corroborates the existence and placement of the two four-voice pieces at ff. 1–7v, although F itself labels them anonymously. [DIAMM F record](https://www.diamm.ac.uk/sources/924/)

The Pérotin-associated repertory is not simply “Léonin plus more open intervals.” Its significant development is:

- expansion from two to three or four voices;
- patterned coordination among the upper voices;
- repeated or rhythmically organized tenor segments in discant;
- stronger sectional construction through modal rhythm, repetitions, rests, and cadential articulations;
- revision of inherited organum through substitute clausulae rather than replacement of chant as foundation.

### 3.3 Chronology and named feast dates

*Viderunt omnes* is often connected with Christmas celebrations around 1198 and *Sederunt principes* with St Stephen’s feast in 1199. These datings rely on the intersection of liturgical records, episcopal regulation, and stylistic attribution; Anonymous IV names the works but does not supply those modern calendar datings.

Accordingly:

- **High confidence:** four-voice settings of these chants survive and Anonymous IV associates them with Pérotin.
- **Medium confidence:** composition or performance around the commonly proposed 1198/1199 occasions.
- **Low confidence:** an exact premiere, exact personnel, or one definitive performance version.

### 3.4 Preset’s selected period

The preset should reference the **shared Notre-Dame Magnus-liber tradition**, approximately the Léonin-associated duplum layer through Pérotin-associated clausula revision and selected tripla/quadrupla.

For a bounded reactive implementation, the safest center is:

> **chant-supported organum duplum with occasional additional consonant voices, informed by but not attempting to recreate Pérotin’s composed tripla and quadrupla.**

That is narrower and more coherent than averaging every surviving work attributed to both names.

---

## 4. Persistent traits versus period-specific traits

### 4.1 Persistent across the selected intersection

The following recur sufficiently across the relevant Notre-Dame repertory to define the preset’s historical center:

1. **Pre-existing liturgical chant as structural material.**
2. **Voice hierarchy:** a tenor derived from chant and one or more added voices.
3. **Temporal enlargement of chant**, especially prolonged tenor tones or repeated tenor segments.
4. **Perfect consonances as structural anchors**, particularly unison, fifth, and octave; the fourth belongs to the medieval consonance discourse but is context-sensitive in multi-voice sonorities.
5. **Cadential convergence** rather than perpetual static spacing.
6. **Sectional contrast:** plainchant versus polyphony, and sustained-tenor versus discant textures.
7. **Modal pitch organization**, not major/minor functional harmony.
8. **Liturgical and rhetorical pacing**, with expansion tied to chant text and feast.

### 4.2 Léonin-associated or duplum-specific traits

- Predominantly two-voice texture.
- Florid duplum above a very slow chant tenor.
- Flexible or disputed rhythm in organum purum.
- Alternation between organum purum, copula-like transitional behavior, and measured discant.
- A relatively exposed relationship between one tenor note and one extended upper-voice span.

These should not be treated as complete descriptions of Pérotin’s quadrupla.

### 4.3 Pérotin-associated traits

- Three- and four-voice monumental works.
- Multiple active upper voices moving at related rates above the tenor.
- Greater dependence on modal rhythmic patterning and coordinated phrase units.
- Repetition and exchange of patterned material among upper voices.
- Replacement clausulae and repertory revision.
- Dense composite sonorities that cannot be reduced to a single fixed interval stack.

These are piece- and layer-specific, not universal properties of all Notre-Dame organum.

### 4.4 Earlier organum traits deliberately excluded

Constant parallel motion at a fourth or fifth is most strongly associated with descriptions of **earlier organum traditions**, including the ninth-century *enchiriadis* complex. That history contributes to the long background of medieval polyphony, but it is not an adequate summary of the Notre-Dame repertory.

The preset must therefore exclude:

- automatic fixed parallel-fourth or parallel-fifth duplication on every note;
- an implication that Léonin and Pérotin invented or principally practiced elementary parallel organum;
- averaging early parallel organum with Pérotin’s quadrupla merely because both are “medieval.”

---

## 5. Relationship to peers and tradition

### 5.1 Shared vocabulary

Léonin- and Pérotin-associated repertories participate in traditions extending beyond two unique individuals:

- inherited Gregorian and local chant;
- earlier improvised and written polyphony;
- Aquitanian and Parisian experiments with sustained-note polyphony;
- modal rhythm and discant practice;
- collective copying, revision, replacement clausulae, and transmission.

Perfect consonances, chant tenors, and modal organization are therefore **shared historical vocabulary**, not personal signatures.

### 5.2 Documented intersection of the two references

The defensible intersection is not “both liked fourths and fifths.” It is:

1. Anonymous IV places both within the history of the same *Magnus liber* tradition.
2. Pérotin is reported to revise or abbreviate material associated with Léonin and to supply improved clausulae.
3. The major manuscripts preserve different voice-count versions and numerous clausulae around the same chant repertory.
4. Both layers retain chant as the structural point of reference while elaborating it through added voices.
5. Their reported distinction—*organista* versus *discantor*—shows continuity with meaningful specialization, not identical style.

This documented revision relationship is what makes one bounded preset coherent.

### 5.3 Meaningful differences deliberately excluded

The preset should not claim to merge:

- Léonin’s florid two-voice organum-purum timing with Pérotin’s precisely composed multi-upper-voice coordination;
- one-voice-against-tenor improvisatory freedom with four-voice score-specific counterpoint;
- all substitute clausulae with complete organa;
- anonymous layers of F, W1, and W2 into two securely identified personal catalogs.

A static interval generator can evoke only the common structural shell, not these distinctions in full.

### 5.4 Why this is not a generic medieval average

A coherent technique emerges if the preset is bounded to:

> **A slow monophonic line treated as a chant-like tenor, temporally enlarged and answered or crowned by a small number of predominantly upper voices that favor perfect-consonance arrivals while retaining stepwise modal motion and phrase rests.**

This excludes unrelated medieval repertories and captures a documented Notre-Dame relationship: chant foundation, temporal expansion, added polyphony, and structural consonance.

---

## 6. Common caricatures to avoid

### 6.1 “Medieval music means parallel fifths”

This substitutes an elementary textbook account of early organum for the more differentiated Notre-Dame repertory. Parallel perfect intervals can occur, but constant automatic parallelism is not an adequate Léonin/Pérotin model.

### 6.2 “Only fourths, fifths, and octaves occur”

Late-twelfth- and thirteenth-century writers emphasize perfect consonances, and Ernest Sanders quotes an organum treatise stating that knowledge of fourth, fifth, and octave is indispensable to proper discant. That does not mean every sounding verticality must be one of those intervals. Melodic movement creates other intervals between structural arrivals. [Sanders, “Consonance and Rhythm in the Organum of the 12th and 13th Centuries,” *JAMS* 33/2 (1980), pp. 264–286](https://www.examenapium.it/cs/biblio/Sanders1980.pdf)

### 6.3 “The chant is surrounded symmetrically”

The chant is normally the **tenor and lowest structural voice** in this repertory. “Around” is acceptable only as loose product language meaning “in relation to.” It should not imply historical upper-and-lower symmetrical harmonization.

### 6.4 “Pérotin simply added voices to Léonin”

Anonymous IV describes revision, abbreviation, replacement clausulae, and excellence in discant. Pérotin’s associated multi-voice repertory changes rhythmic and contrapuntal organization, not merely voice count.

### 6.5 “The composers and their careers are well documented”

Almost everything commonly said about the two composers rests on a small amount of late testimony plus contested archival identification. Manuscript attributions are not composer signatures.

### 6.6 “Cathedral reverberation explains the style”

The architecture is relevant context, but claims that exact note lengths, rhythms, or compositional devices were caused by Notre-Dame’s acoustics require more evidence than the surviving sources provide.

### 6.7 “Cloister equals Notre-Dame”

The repertory is cathedral-centered. The title may evoke sacred enclosure and resonance, but documentation should say “Notre-Dame organum,” not “authentic cloister chant.”

### 6.8 “A MIDI chord stack reconstructs organum”

A reactive harmonizer lacks the liturgical chant source, notation, composed melismas, replacement clausulae, modal rhythmic organization, singer practice, tuning, and manuscript-specific form necessary for reconstruction.

---

## 7. Primary and near-primary evidence

### 7.1 Anonymous IV on Léonin and Pérotin

Anonymous IV’s famous passage reports, in substance:

- Magister Leoninus was an excellent *organista*;
- he made a great book of organa from Gradual and Antiphonal chants to enlarge divine service;
- the book remained in use until the time of Perotinus Magnus;
- Pérotin, an excellent *discantor*, abbreviated or revised it and made better clausulae or *puncta*;
- Pérotin made the four-voice *Viderunt* and *Sederunt*, along with named three-voice works.

**Citation:** Anonymous IV, *De mensuris et discantu*, ed. Fritz Reckow, *Der Musiktraktat des Anonymus 4*, vol. 1 (Wiesbaden, 1967), pp. 45–46. See Edward H. Roesner, “Who ‘Made’ the *Magnus Liber*?”, *Early Music History* 20 (2001), especially the opening quotation and discussion. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0261127901001061) · [PDF](http://www.examenapium.it/cs/biblio/Roesner2001.pdf)

**Interpretive caution:** Roesner questions treating “making” the *Magnus liber* as straightforward sole authorship. The surviving book is better understood as a layered repertory shaped by compilation, transmission, and revision.

### 7.2 Florence F: four-voice works

- *Viderunt omnes*, F ff. 1–4.
- *Sederunt principes*, F ff. 4–7v.

Both are transmitted in four voices at the head of F. Their manuscript presence strongly corroborates Anonymous IV’s identification of a conspicuous quadruplum repertory, while the manuscript’s anonymity prevents treating it as direct autograph evidence. [DIAMM F contents](https://www.diamm.ac.uk/sources/924/)

Mark Everist’s transcription project provides a modern score resource:

- **Fascicle 1:** “Organa, Conductus a4, Clausulae a4 and a3.” [DIAMM edition portal](https://www.diamm.ac.uk/resources/music-editions/organa-and-clausulae-ms-i-fl-pluteus-291/)

For these pieces, manuscript folios are more stable references than modern bar numbers, which vary by editorial rhythmic realization.

### 7.3 Florence F: two-voice counterparts

- *Viderunt omnes*, F ff. 99–100v.
- *Sederunt*, F ff. 101–102.
- *Alleluia Pascha nostrum*, F ff. 109–109v.

These folios show why the repertory cannot be represented by the four-voice monuments alone. F preserves a substantial two-voice chant-based organum corpus alongside its tripla and quadrupla. [DIAMM F contents](https://www.diamm.ac.uk/sources/924/)

### 7.4 Clausula evidence

F’s later two-voice fascicles contain numerous short settings on individual tenor words or syllables—multiple versions of *Dominus*, *In saeculum*, *Nostrum*, *Latus est*, and others. This materially supports a culture of alternate or substitute clausulae rather than a single fixed harmonization for an entire chant. See especially the dense contents listings around F ff. 147–184v. [DIAMM F contents](https://www.diamm.ac.uk/sources/924/)

### 7.5 Treatise evidence for perfect consonances

Sanders’s survey quotes a twelfth-century organum instruction that a maker of discant must know the fourth, fifth, and octave because proper discant is constructed through them. This supports treating perfect intervals as indispensable structural vocabulary.

**Citation:** Ernest H. Sanders, “Consonance and Rhythm in the Organum of the 12th and 13th Centuries,” *Journal of the American Musicological Society* 33, no. 2 (Summer 1980): 264–286. [Accessible PDF](https://www.examenapium.it/cs/biblio/Sanders1980.pdf)

It does **not** establish that every note in Notre-Dame organum is harmonized by a static perfect interval.

### 7.6 Score-based scholarship on organum duplum

Yampolsky’s corpus analysis finds that modal organization, pitch affinities, and consonance all help explain duplum construction. The result argues against reducing the upper voice to one constant transposition of the tenor.

**Citation:** Asher Vijay Yampolsky, *Melodic Mode in Notre Dame Organum Duplum*, PhD diss., University of Southampton, 2020, 294 pp.; especially chapters 1 and 5 as summarized in the institutional abstract. [University record](https://eprints.soton.ac.uk/482281/)

### 7.7 Cultural function of tripla and quadrupla

Gross treats the elaboration of tripla and quadrupla as a culturally situated, virtuosic practice for major feasts.

**Citation:** Guillaume Gross, “Organum at Notre-Dame in the Twelfth and Thirteenth Centuries: Rhetoric in Words and Music,” *Plainsong and Medieval Music* 15, no. 2 (2006): 87–108. [DOI and abstract](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0961137106000349)

---

## 8. Evaluation of the catalog promise

### Promise

> “Open fourths, fifths, and octaves around a chant line.”

### 8.1 Historically defensible components

**Defensible with qualification:**

- **Chant line:** strongly defensible. The organum repertory is structurally based on liturgical chant.
- **Open fifths and octaves:** defensible as prominent structural consonances, especially for beginnings, arrivals, and cadential stability.
- **Fourths:** defensible as part of medieval consonance theory and two-voice discant vocabulary, but treatment depends on voice context and texture.
- **Slow held line:** defensible as an evocation of sustained-tenor organum purum.
- **Sparse phrase rests:** defensible as a modern analogue for sectional articulation and alternation with chant.

### 8.2 Misleading implications

The promise becomes misleading if implemented or described as:

- constant parallel fourths, fifths, and octaves;
- a three-note “power-chord” stack on every MIDI input;
- symmetric voices both above and below a central chant;
- chord-by-chord harmonization of a freely improvised modern melody;
- a model equally representative of Léonin’s duplum and Pérotin’s quadrupla;
- evidence that only perfect intervals sounded.

### 8.3 Recommended historical wording

A safer result description is:

> **“A slow chant-like line is prolonged beneath sparse organal voices that favor open fifths and octaves, with occasional fourths and modal stepwise motion.”**

If product brevity requires the original wording, supporting copy should add:

> **“A bounded modern evocation of Notre-Dame organum, not a reconstruction of Léonin or Pérotin.”**

---

## 9. What a modern reactive MIDI approximation must not claim

The preset must not claim:

1. **Authentic reconstruction.** It does not read a historical chant, manuscript, or liturgical occasion.
2. **Composer imitation.** It cannot recreate Léonin’s composed duplum melodies or Pérotin’s score-specific upper-voice counterpoint.
3. **Authentic rhythm.** Organum-purum rhythm and editorial realization remain contested; reactive MIDI imposes modern timing.
4. **Authentic tuning.** Equal-tempered MIDI is not evidence for medieval interval tuning or vocal intonation.
5. **Authentic voice disposition.** The player’s line may function as a practical input proxy, not necessarily as a historically transmitted tenor.
6. **Authentic form.** True organa alternate chant, organum purum, discant, clausulae, and cadences according to specific liturgical melodies and texts.
7. **Authentic venue or ensemble.** Reverb, organ patches, choirs, or “cloister” imagery do not establish Notre-Dame performance conditions.
8. **A complete Léonin–Pérotin synthesis.** The implementation captures only their repertories’ documented intersection.

An honest approximation statement is:

> **“Cloister Organum uses slow input as a chant-like tenor and adds bounded, predominantly upper voices favoring structural perfect consonances. It evokes one shared feature of the Notre-Dame organum repertory; it does not reconstruct medieval scores, rhythm, tuning, liturgy, or the personal styles of Léonin and Pérotin.”**

---

## 10. Confidence and gaps

### 10.1 Claim-level confidence

| Claim | Confidence | Basis / limitation |
|---|---|---|
| Notre-Dame organum elaborates pre-existing liturgical chant | **High** | Treatise testimony, repertory contents, and surviving tenor texts |
| Organum duplum is central to the repertory | **High** | Large surviving corpus in F/W1/W2 and modern score-based scholarship |
| Perfect fourths, fifths, and octaves are important theoretical consonances | **High** | Contemporary/near-contemporary treatise tradition and Sanders’s source study |
| Constant perfect-interval parallelism describes Notre-Dame organum | **High confidence that this is false** | Scores and scholarship show differentiated upper melodies, sectional styles, and other verticalities |
| Léonin made a great book of organum and Pérotin revised it | **Medium** | Explicit Anonymous IV report, but written decades later and challenged as a literal authorship history |
| F’s complete two-voice corpus is substantially Léonin’s personal work | **Low to medium** | Conventional association, not manuscript attribution or autograph proof |
| *Viderunt* and *Sederunt* quadrupla are by Pérotin | **Medium to high** | Named by Anonymous IV and matched to exceptional surviving four-voice works; still not autographs |
| Exact performances occurred at Christmas 1198 and St Stephen 1199 | **Medium** | Plausible documentary reconstruction, not stated in the musical manuscripts or Anonymous IV |
| Léonin and Pérotin had a documented teacher–student relationship | **Low** | Repertory succession is documented; personal pedagogy is not securely established |
| Cathedral acoustics directly determined the style | **Low** | Plausible context but insufficient for causal claims |
| Equal-tempered open stacks reproduce medieval consonance | **Low** | Modern technical approximation, not historical tuning evidence |

### 10.2 Unresolved gaps

1. **Authorship boundaries:** The exact share of the surviving *Magnus liber* attributable to either named figure remains unresolved.
2. **Biography:** Léonin’s and Pérotin’s identities, offices, dates, and career sequences are only partially reconstructable.
3. **Rhythm of organum purum:** Treatises and notation permit competing modern realizations.
4. **Tuning and vocal execution:** Manuscripts do not prescribe a single modern reproducible temperament, ensemble size, or timbre.
5. **Fourth treatment:** “Fourth” cannot safely become an unrestricted lowest-voice sonority rule across all multi-voice textures.
6. **Modern measure numbers:** Editorial bar numbering varies. Manuscript folios and named sections are the more reliable traceability references.
7. **Liturgy-to-interaction translation:** A player-generated melody is not automatically equivalent to a historically authorized chant tenor.

### 10.3 Recommended validation before implementation

For parent synthesis, compare any proposed interval algorithm against short passages from:

- F ff. 99–100v, two-voice *Viderunt omnes*;
- F ff. 109–109v, two-voice *Alleluia Pascha nostrum*;
- F ff. 1–4, four-voice *Viderunt omnes*;
- F ff. 4–7v, four-voice *Sederunt principes*.

The test is not exact note reproduction. It is whether the implementation preserves the historically bounded thesis—**slow structural tenor, independently shaped upper motion, selective perfect-consonance arrivals, and cadential convergence**—rather than emitting permanent parallel stacks.

---

## Sources

### Kept

- **Anonymous IV, *De mensuris et discantu***, ed. Fritz Reckow, *Der Musiktraktat des Anonymus 4*, vol. 1, pp. 45–46 — principal near-contemporary testimony naming Léonin, Pérotin, the *Magnus liber*, and named multi-voice works.
- **Edward H. Roesner, “Who ‘Made’ the *Magnus Liber*?”** ([DOI](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0261127901001061); [PDF](http://www.examenapium.it/cs/biblio/Roesner2001.pdf)) — authoritative critique of simplistic single-composer authorship and careful translation of Anonymous IV.
- **DIAMM, Florence MS Pluteus 29.1** (https://www.diamm.ac.uk/sources/924/) — institutional manuscript catalog, folio references, voice counts, and facsimile access.
- **DIAMM, W1** (https://www.diamm.ac.uk/sources/870/) and **W2** (https://www.diamm.ac.uk/sources/854/) — authoritative records for the other principal Notre-Dame witnesses.
- **Mark Everist/DIAMM, transcriptions from F** (https://www.diamm.ac.uk/resources/music-editions/organa-and-clausulae-ms-i-fl-pluteus-291/) — current score-based scholarly resource with explicit editorial limitations.
- **Ernest H. Sanders, “Consonance and Rhythm in the Organum of the 12th and 13th Centuries”** (https://www.examenapium.it/cs/biblio/Sanders1980.pdf) — source-based evidence for consonance vocabulary and rhythmic practice.
- **Asher Vijay Yampolsky, *Melodic Mode in Notre Dame Organum Duplum*** (https://eprints.soton.ac.uk/482281/) — institutional, corpus-based analysis of modal and dronal organization.
- **Guillaume Gross, “Organum at Notre-Dame…”** (https://doi.org/10.1017/S0961137106000349) — scholarly account of tripla/quadrupla as virtuosic festal elaboration.
- **Johannes de Garlandia, *De mensurabili musica*** ([critical edition](https://www.examenapium.it/meri/pdf/Reimer1.pdf); [translation catalog](https://archive.org/details/concerningmeasur0000joha)) — central theoretical witness for measured polyphony and rhythmic modes.

### Dropped

- **Wikipedia summaries of Léonin, Pérotin, Anonymous IV, and the *Magnus liber*** — useful discovery aids but unnecessary where primary editions and institutional catalogs are available.
- **Scribd/PDFCoffee classroom analyses of *Alleluia Pascha nostrum*** — unclear provenance and weaker authority than manuscripts, critical editions, and university scholarship.
- **General music-appreciation pages describing organum as parallel fourths or fifths** — conflate early parallel organum with the later Notre-Dame repertory.
- **Blogs and unsourced listening guides to *Viderunt* or *Sederunt*** — excluded where claims could be grounded in F, Anonymous IV, or peer-reviewed scholarship.
- **Modern acoustical or architectural reconstructions** — potentially valuable for a separate performance report, but insufficient as primary evidence for compositional rules.

---

## Historical decision

**Suitable only as a bounded approximation.**

The two named references have a documented and coherent intersection in the Notre-Dame *Magnus liber* tradition, but the current catalog wording needs qualification. Preserve chant foundation, temporal expansion, selective perfect-consonance anchoring, upper-voice hierarchy, and phrase-level cadence. Reject constant parallel stacks and any claim of authentic Léonin/Pérotin reconstruction.

text:
# Research: Preset 01 — Cloister Organum  
## Music theory and temporal behavior

## Summary

A defensible Notre-Dame preset must not reduce Léonin and Pérotin to parallel fourths. The repertory alternates three materially different behaviors: **organum purum** (a freely flowing duplum over a sustained chant tone), **discant/clausula** (both voices measured in rhythmic modes), and **triplum/quadruplum** (two or three rhythmically coordinated upper voices over a much slower chant tenor). The smallest honest Contrapunk implementation is therefore a bounded **two-voice, chant-tenor organum-purum approximation** using modal pitch material, long input holds, predominantly perfect-consonance arrivals, and phrase rests; explicit interval-stack selection and sectional rhythmic-state switching remain named gaps.

---

## 1. Scope and corpus

### Selected repertory

This report draws its rules from:

- two-voice *Magnus liber organi* repertory associated by the later testimony of Anonymous IV with **Léonin**, especially organa dupla such as *Viderunt omnes* and the broader W1/F/W2 transmitted corpus;
- the Notre-Dame repertory of **two-part discant clausulae**, including substitute clausula practice;
- the three- and four-voice repertory associated with **Pérotin**, especially *Viderunt omnes* and *Sederunt principes*, plus the larger tripla/quadrupla practice.

The repertory survives chiefly in the manuscript complexes commonly called W1, F, and W2. The modern *Magnus Liber Organi* edition itself reflects materially different editorial decisions about the underdetermined rhythm of sustained-tenor passages. [Turner, “Notre Dame Organum Duplum”](https://www.musicandpractice.org/volume-1/notre-dame-organum-duplum-modern-edition/)

### Attribution caution

Anonymous IV’s account linking Léonin with the *Magnus liber* and Pérotin with revisions and large-scale tripla/quadrupla was written decades later. “Léonin style” and “Pérotin style” are useful repertorial labels, not secure modern authorship metadata. Scholarship also emphasizes compilation, oral practice, substitution, and reuse rather than a fixed authored work in the modern sense. [Bradley, “Who ‘Made’ the Magnus Liber?”](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0261127901001061)

**Preset scope:** late-twelfth-/early-thirteenth-century Parisian liturgical organum, with the operational baseline centered on **organum duplum/purum**, not a claim to reproduce every Notre-Dame texture.

**Confidence:** High for the three-way stylistic distinction; medium for individual attributions.

---

## 2. Three practices that must remain separate

| Practice | Tenor behavior | Added-voice behavior | Rhythmic organization | Operational identity |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Organum purum / organum per se** | One chant pitch sustained for a long span | One florid duplum, usually above it | Rhythm underdetermined/free; ligatures shape gestures without proving one continuous rhythmic mode | Drone-like span, but with responsive intervallic articulation |
| **Discant / clausula** | Chant melisma segmented into repeated/measured notes | Duplum rhythmically active against tenor | Modal, measurable rhythm; phrases/ordines bounded by rests | Propulsive two-part rhythmic counterpoint |
| **Organum triplum/quadruplum / cum alio** | Very slow chant foundation | Two or three upper voices moving at broadly comparable rates | Upper voices coordinated through modal rhythmic organization | Layered upper-voice polyphony, not parallel interval duplication |

Organum purum’s free rhythm remains disputed in detail, but modern performers and editors broadly distinguish it from the more securely measurable discant passages. Turner warns that forcing sustained-tenor passages into a fixed “lilting” modal rhythm destroys their flexibility. [Turner](https://www.musicandpractice.org/volume-1/notre-dame-organum-duplum-modern-edition/); [Yudkin, “The Rhythm of Organum Purum”](https://doi.org/10.2307/763685)

Pérotin-generation “organum cum alio” adds voices that move at the duplum’s rate rather than at the tenor’s rate; consequently, the added voices are in discant with one another even while all unfold above the slow chant. [Taruskin, “Organum cum alio”](https://www.oxfordwesternmusic.com/view/Volume1/actrade-9780195384819-div1-006005.xml)

**Confidence:** High.

---

## 3. Tonal center, modality, chromaticism, and tuning

### 3.1 Tonal organization

1. The lowest voice is a pre-existing chant, not a generated functional bass.
2. Pitch organization derives from medieval chant modality, recurrent melodic outlines, finals, reciting/focal pitches, and the locally sustained tenor pitch.
3. The current tenor pitch creates a temporary **dronal center**, while the work’s chant mode supplies the larger pitch hierarchy.
4. A modern “key + scale” is only an approximation: mode cannot be inferred reliably from the final alone, and individual chants may change local orientation.

Yampolsky’s corpus analysis argues that organum-purum melodic material is primarily mode-dependent, while also finding a strong local dronal hearing and one analytical dimension better explained by consonance. [Yampolsky, *Melodic Mode in Notre Dame Organum Duplum*](https://eprints.soton.ac.uk/482281/)

### 3.2 Operational rule

- Require a user-selected chant final/mode approximation.
- Keep the pitch collection diatonic by default.
- Treat the held input as the **local tenor reference**, not automatically as a new tonic on every note.
- Do not introduce functional dominant–tonic progressions, major/minor chord syntax, blues chromaticism, or automatic modal interchange.
- Musica ficta and B-flat/B-natural choices are source- and context-dependent; they should not be randomized by a preset.

### 3.3 Tuning

The notation does not prescribe a single modern tuning standard. Pythagorean-leaning intonation is historically plausible for perfect intervals, but exact pitch, temperament, ensemble composition, and ficta remain performance decisions. The preset should prioritize pure-sounding unisons, fifths, fourths, and octaves if microtuning ever becomes available, but must not advertise an exact historical temperament.

**Confidence:**  
- Modal/dronal organization: High.  
- Exact ficta per generic preset: Low.  
- Pythagorean tuning as one defensible realization: Medium.

**Competing interpretation:** Mode-centered and consonance-centered analyses are not mutually exclusive; modal melodic design governs the line while consonance governs important vertical meetings.

---

## 4. Interval and sonority vocabulary

### 4.1 Organum purum

- Structural arrivals favor **unison, octave, fifth, and contextually fourth-related perfect consonances**.
- The duplum may pass through seconds, thirds, sixths, and sevenths during its florid motion; these are events in a line, not a modern chord vocabulary.
- Dissonance should be brief or directed, not held as an unexplained stable sonority.
- Long durations and phrase boundaries should disproportionately coincide with consonant vertical meetings.

Sanders relates rhythmic weight and note length in organum to consonant coordination: consonance can identify structurally important “meetings,” rather than every instantaneous vertical interval being equally stable. [Sanders, “Consonance and Rhythm in the Organum of the 12th and 13th Centuries”](https://doi.org/10.2307/831113)

### 4.2 Discant/clausula

- Consonance is coordinated with measured rhythmic positions.
- Dissonance may arise on intervening events but should lead to a consonant boundary or phrase-ending sonority.
- Repeated tenor patterns permit recurring sonority cycles.
- Avoid interpreting these cycles as chord progressions; clausula composition explores “harmonic sounds in measured time,” not functional harmony. [Bradley, *Creating Clausulae at Notre-Dame-de-Paris*](https://www.repository.cam.ac.uk/items/09fe45cf-e487-467e-aeea-575d40f0fb28)

### 4.3 Triplum/quadruplum

- Sonority must be evaluated among **all sounding voices**, not only each voice against the tenor.
- A safe perfect interval from each generated voice to its immediate predecessor can still create a tritone or harsh compound against another voice.
- Upper voices need independent but mutually coordinated contours and rhythms.
- Doubling at unison or octave is permissible, but continuously cloning one contour at fixed intervals erases upper-voice independence.

### Testable tension/resolution rule

At phrase attacks and cadences, require a perfect consonance against the tenor. Within the phrase, permit weaker intervals only on shorter events and require stepwise or small-leap departure toward a subsequent perfect-consonance arrival.

**Confidence:** High for perfect-consonance structural priority; medium for any fixed machine-readable list applying identically across all manuscripts and textures.

---

## 5. Spacing, inversion, doubling, and register

### Organum purum

- Tenor is the lower foundational voice.
- Duplum is predominantly above it, but voice crossing should not be declared impossible.
- A practical initial spacing is unison, fourth, fifth, or octave, expanding and contracting through the phrase.
- Avoid a permanently fixed octave-plus-fifth “power chord.”
- Avoid placing the florid voice several octaves away throughout; registral contrast should remain singable and relational.

### Discant/clausula

- Voices remain sufficiently close for audible contrapuntal exchange.
- Repeated tenor cells may occupy a compact range while the duplum traces a larger arch.
- Cadential convergence to unison or octave is more characteristic than ending on a modern complete triad.

### Triplum/quadruplum

- The chant remains lowest in the normative texture.
- Upper voices occupy overlapping ranges and may cross.
- Upper voices should not be mechanically assigned “root, fifth, octave” roles.
- Doubling should be episodic; independent melodic parts are the defining behavior.

### Operational register target

For MIDI realization, place the tenor roughly in a low-to-middle male vocal register and keep the first added voice approximately within an octave or twelfth above it. Three-/four-part simulation needs bounded individual ranges and voice-crossing support, not only global octave spreading.

**Confidence:** Medium; exact ranges vary by item and performance transposition.

---

## 6. Melodic contour, motives, repetition, transformation, ornament

### Organum purum

- Florid upper gestures elaborate one held tenor pitch.
- Prefer conjunct motion, short turns around modal focal tones, neighboring motion, and occasional controlled leaps followed by compensating motion.
- Ligature groupings imply perceptible gesture units even where exact duration is disputed.
- Repetition should be formulaic and varied, not a literal DAW loop.
- Ornament is structural melodic elaboration; it should not become chromatic jazz embellishment.

### Discant/clausula

- Motivic cells may recur because tenor rhythmic units recur.
- Upper-voice material can be designed in sustained, interconnected spans and may contribute substantially to overall clausula form rather than merely reacting note-by-note to the tenor. [Bradley, *Creating Clausulae*](https://www.repository.cam.ac.uk/items/09fe45cf-e487-467e-aeea-575d40f0fb28)
- Repetition may preserve rhythm while changing contour or preserve contour while changing its position against the tenor.

### Triplum/quadruplum

- Upper voices should exchange short figures, overlap, and complement one another.
- Identical simultaneous contours are a special event, not a default.
- Density comes from coordinated independent parts, not from chordal attacks on every input note.

**Confidence:** Medium-high.

---

## 7. Voice motion and layer interaction

### Organum purum

- The tenor’s apparent stillness creates **oblique motion** as the default relation.
- Duplum motion may repeatedly depart from and return to consonance.
- The tenor is not an inert electronic drone: its attacks, duration, releases, and transitions articulate the phrase and should respond to the upper line. Turner specifically criticizes performance that treats the tenor as an unrelated drone beneath ornament. [Turner](https://www.musicandpractice.org/volume-1/notre-dame-organum-duplum-modern-edition/)
- Parallel perfect motion may occur and must not be prohibited by later Renaissance counterpoint rules.

### Discant/clausula

- Both parts are active.
- Contrary, oblique, similar, and parallel motion are all available.
- Rhythmic coordination matters more than enforcing later species-counterpoint prohibitions.
- The tenor’s repeated modal pattern and duplum phrase must share boundaries.

### Triplum/quadruplum

- Upper voices are mutually independent.
- One voice may sustain while another moves; voices may use complementary modal patterns.
- Motion must be checked pairwise and against the total sonority.
- A cascade in which voice 3 is generated only from voice 2 is insufficient: voice 3 must also account for tenor and voice 1.

**Confidence:** High that later “no parallel fifths/octaves” rules are misleading here.

---

## 8. Rhythm, meter, subdivision, accent, and phase

### 8.1 Organum purum

- Do **not** quantize the duplum into an unbroken rhythmic mode.
- Use breath-shaped, unequal gesture lengths.
- Let consonant arrivals, ligature-like groups, and the imminent tenor change influence duration.
- No swing.
- No modern recurring backbeat.
- Silence separates phrase units.

The precise rhythm is a major scholarly and editorial dispute. Yudkin rejects a blanket modal reading; modern editors range from neutral note values to rhythmically suggestive transcriptions. Turner favors flexible performance informed by the source ligatures. [Yudkin](https://doi.org/10.2307/763685); [Turner](https://www.musicandpractice.org/volume-1/notre-dame-organum-duplum-modern-edition/)

### 8.2 Discant/clausula

- Transport is required for an honest simulation.
- Use a repeating long/short modal pattern within an **ordo**, not an indefinitely running groove.
- Modes I and II—long–short and short–long relationships in modern abstraction—are useful minimal defaults, but the historical system contains six modes and manuscript notation permits qualifications and irregularities.
- Phrase-ending rests reset the pattern.
- Accents follow the long positions and consonant meetings, not a modern 4/4 measure.

The University of Basel’s notation resource describes the six modal patterns as phrase-level organizations recognized through ligature sequences. [University of Basel, “Rhythmic patterns”](https://tales.nmc.unibas.ch/en/from-ink-to-sound-32/coordination-in-rhythm-modal-notation-189/rhythmic-patterns-how-to-recognise-a-mode-957)

### 8.3 Triplum/quadruplum

- Multiple upper voices may share or complement modal patterns.
- Their phrase lengths must align often enough to produce clear structural arrivals.
- The tenor advances on a much slower timescale.
- This is coordinated polyrhythmic layering within modal mensuration, not free asynchronous note spawning.

**Confidence:**  
- Discant’s measured/modal character: High.  
- Exact realization of organum-purum rhythm: Low–medium.  
- One fixed rhythmic mode for all Pérotin works: Low.

---

## 9. Phrase, cadence, density, silence, and formal pacing

### Phrase scale

Absolute bar counts are a modern overlay. Define phrases by:

- one held tenor pitch or tenor segment;
- an upper-voice gesture/ordo;
- a consonant arrival;
- a rest or chant-tone change.

### Cadence behavior

- Reduce melodic activity near the cadence.
- Approach a perfect consonance by step or controlled contrary/oblique motion.
- Prefer unison or octave as the strongest terminal simplification; fifths can serve as intermediate or less final arrivals.
- Release together or leave a brief clean silence before the next tenor attack.
- Do not append a leading-tone dominant chord.

### Density

- Organum purum: one sustained tenor plus one florid voice.
- Clausula: two active measured voices.
- Triplum/quadruplum: slow tenor plus two/three active upper voices.
- Liturgical plainchant alternates with polyphonic solo sections; continuous maximum-density polyphony is misleading.

**Confidence:** High at texture level; medium for a universal cadence-ranking rule.

---

## 10. Dynamics and articulation

The manuscripts do not encode modern dynamics, but arrangement behavior should reflect vocal phrasing:

- soft or clear tenor onset, then sustained support;
- connected upper-voice gestures with subtle local emphasis at long notes and consonant arrivals;
- slight taper before a rest or tenor change;
- no piano-like repeated hard attacks on a sustained organal voice;
- no automatic velocity crescendo on every phrase;
- discant may be more incisive than organum purum, but remains vocal rather than percussive.

In a reverberant realization, articulation must preserve separable entries and cadence silence. Cathedral acoustics should not be used as an excuse for indistinct note lifecycle or permanent sustain.

**Confidence:** Medium; these are performance-derived operational recommendations rather than explicit notational instructions.

---

## 11. Temporal behavior

### 11.1 Within-phrase evolution

#### Organum purum

`Perfect-consonance attack → florid expansion → local consonant plateaus → registral/ornamental peak → contraction → perfect-consonance cadence → breath`

Triggers:

- **Attack:** new long tenor note after silence.
- **Expansion:** tenor held beyond one pulse or threshold duration.
- **Peak:** elapsed hold time, rising input intensity, or accumulated upper gestures.
- **Cadence preparation:** imminent tenor release, reduced player velocity, or phrase-rest detection.
- **Reset:** tenor release plus minimum silence.

#### Discant/clausula

`Measured pickup → stable rhythmic-mode cycle → one or more repeated/varied ordines → cadence lengthening → rest`

Triggers:

- transport running;
- chant melisma or explicitly selected discant section;
- phrase count or player release requests cadence;
- rest resets the modal pattern.

#### Triplum/quadruplum

`Tenor attack → staged upper entries → interlocking density → coordinated upper-voice arrival → tenor advance`

Triggers:

- long tenor hold permits additional upper entry;
- phrase boundary aligns voices;
- density ceiling prevents further entry;
- tenor change clears or re-targets upper parts.

### 11.2 Across-section evolution

A defensible full arrangement would use:

`Plainchant/solo → organum purum → copula-like intensification → discant/clausula → cadence/rest → return or expanded triplum/quadruplum`

The transition is linked historically to chant texture: sustained-tenor organum and measured discant are not random “variation scenes.” Clausulae can replace measured segments, and later repertorial transmission preserves multiple alternatives.

### 11.3 Repertory evolution

- Earlier/Léonin-associated repertory foregrounds two-voice organum duplum alternating sustained-tenor organum with discant.
- Pérotin-associated practice expands and revises the repertory, develops substitute clausulae, and creates large-scale three-/four-part pieces.
- Added voices change the compositional problem: rhythmic coordination and all-voice sonority replace a simple tenor–duplum relation.
- Later clausula reuse leads toward the motet, where added texts and greater layer differentiation produce another distinct genre.

This is an evolution of available practices, not a clean replacement of “primitive parallel organum” by “advanced chords.”

**Confidence:** High for broad development; medium for a strict composer-by-composer chronology.

---

## 12. Testable stylistic invariants

1. **Chant foundation:** The lowest/foundational voice is a slow modal line, not a functional bass progression.
2. **Section distinction:** Organum purum, discant/clausula, and triplum/quadruplum must not share one undifferentiated algorithm.
3. **Organum-purum obliquity:** During a long tenor hold, the added line produces multiple notes or a shaped gesture rather than one static chord only.
4. **Structural perfect consonance:** Phrase attacks and endings resolve to unison, fourth/fifth-related, or octave sonorities appropriate to the texture.
5. **Directed dissonance:** Non-perfect vertical intervals occur as shorter connective events, not arbitrary sustained endpoints.
6. **Modal containment:** Output remains within the configured chant-mode approximation unless an explicitly defined ficta rule applies.
7. **No functional cadence:** Phrase endings do not generate V–I chord syntax or raised-leading-tone behavior automatically.
8. **Rhythmic separation:** Organum purum remains flexibly timed; discant is transport-locked and modal-patterned.
9. **Breath/reset:** Phrase rests terminate or reset the generated pattern and release all generated notes.
10. **Independent added voices:** In triplum/quadruplum, upper voices are not constant transpositions or simultaneous duplicates.
11. **Tenor responsiveness:** The tenor attack, change, and release govern generated phrase state.
12. **Bounded density:** Maximum texture is one tenor plus the historically selected number of added voices; no Mirror-generated note cloud.
13. **Parallel-perfect permission:** Later prohibitions on parallel fifths/octaves must not be imposed as universal rules.
14. **All-pairs validation:** Three-/four-voice sonorities must be checked globally, not only along a chained generation path.

---

## 13. Parameters that may vary without losing identity

- chant final and modal family;
- tenor transposition and practical vocal register;
- duplum range, provided it remains relational to the tenor;
- relative frequency of fourths, fifths, unisons, and octaves;
- amount and location of connective dissonance;
- organum-purum gesture length and rubato;
- selected rhythmic mode and tempo for clausulae;
- number of repeated ordines before cadence;
- two, three, or four voices when the corresponding texture algorithm exists;
- degree of voice crossing;
- upper-voice entry staggering;
- phrase length and silence duration;
- performance temperament and modest ficta choices;
- reverberation, timbre, and ensemble size, if not presented as historically exact.

---

## 14. Misleading behaviors and rejected shortcuts

1. **Continuous parallel fourths:** evokes generic early organum caricature, not Notre-Dame organum purum.
2. **Power-chord generator:** a fixed root–fifth–octave block suppresses florid motion and sectional change.
3. **Chained fourth stacks:** can yield unintended tritones between nonadjacent voices and does not model Pérotin’s independent upper parts.
4. **Renaissance species counterpoint:** automatic rejection of parallel fifths/octaves imports later norms.
5. **Modern triadic harmonization:** thirds-stacked seventh chords are foreign to the selected behavior.
6. **Functional tonal cadence:** dominant–tonic inference misrepresents modal chant organization.
7. **One rhythmic mode everywhere:** especially misleading in organum purum.
8. **Random consonant-below mode:** random thirds through sevenths lacks phrase direction and historical tenor/duplum roles.
9. **Electronic drone plus unrelated noodling:** the tenor must articulate and interact with consonance points.
10. **Mirror octave multiplication:** creates unhistorical automatic doublings and excessive density.
11. **All voices attacking every input:** Pérotin’s added voices require temporal independence.
12. **Permanent four-voice density:** erases alternation with chant, duplum, and rests.
13. **Automatic chromatic borrowing:** modal interchange is not a substitute for source-sensitive ficta.
14. **Claimed exact imitation:** the current reactive engine cannot reconstruct chant-derived phrase form, ligature rhythm, substitute clausulae, or manuscript variation.

---

## 15. Abstract acceptance examples

Scale degrees refer to a seven-note chant-mode approximation; `T` is tenor, `D` duplum, and beats are modern test coordinates rather than claims about original barring.

### Example A — organum purum: one tenor tone, free upper arc

**Input**

```text
Mode approximation: Dorian
T: degree 1, beat 0.0–8.0
Then silence: beat 8.0–9.5
```

**Acceptable abstract output**

```text
D:
beat 0.0   degree 5   (perfect-consonance attack)
beat 1.2   degree 6
beat 1.8   degree 5
beat 2.7   degree 4
beat 3.1   degree 2
beat 4.3   degree 4
beat 5.0   degree 5   (local plateau)
beat 6.1   degree 7
beat 6.7   degree 6
beat 7.5   degree 1'  (octave cadence)
release by beat 8.0
```

**Assertions**

- tenor remains unchanged for the span;
- duplum rhythm is unequal rather than a repeated long–short loop;
- connective intervals are shorter than structural fifth/octave arrivals;
- all generated notes stop at input release;
- no note occurs during the phrase rest.

### Example B — discant/clausula: measured repeated ordo

**Input**

```text
Transport: running, ternary pulse
T chant segment: 1, 2, 1, 7, 1
Tenor attacks: beats 0, 1.5, 3, 4.5, 6
Phrase rest after beat 7.5
```

**Acceptable abstract output**

```text
D rhythmic mode: long–short, reset at phrase rest

beat 0.0   degree 5   long
beat 1.0   degree 4   short
beat 1.5   degree 6   long
beat 2.5   degree 5   short
beat 3.0   degree 5   long
beat 4.0   degree 3   short
beat 4.5   degree 2   long
beat 5.5   degree 7   short
beat 6.0   degree 3   long
beat 7.0   degree 1'  cadence
```

**Assertions**

- output aligns with transport;
- rhythmic pattern repeats within the ordo;
- terminal event is consonant and lengthened;
- rest resets phase before the next phrase;
- stopping transport releases the lane.

### Example C — abstract triplum, showing why fixed stacks fail

**Input**

```text
T: degree 1 held beats 0–6
```

**Acceptable relational output**

```text
D:  beat 0 degree 5 → beat 2 degree 4 → beat 4 degree 5 → beat 5.5 degree 1'
Tr: beat 1 degree 1' → beat 2.5 degree 7 → beat 3.5 degree 6 → beat 5.5 degree 5
```

**Assertions**

- upper voices enter at different times;
- contours differ;
- both coordinate at beat 5.5;
- output is not `[T, T+4th, previous+4th]`;
- every simultaneous sonority is validated across T–D, T–Tr, and D–Tr.

---

## 16. Mapping to current Contrapunk capabilities

### 16.1 HarmonyEngine capabilities verified in supplied code

| Requirement | Current capability | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| Modal pitch collection | `Key` plus seven diatonic `ScaleMode` variants | **Partial:** useful modern approximation, not medieval modal grammar |
| Two-to-four voices | `voice_count`, `voice_position` | **Available structurally** |
| Place input as tenor | set player at bottom `voice_position` | **Available** |
| Diatonic fourth relation | `HarmonyMode::DiatonicFourths` | **Partial and misleading if used alone** |
| Fifth relation | No explicit diatonic-fifth mode or per-voice interval list | **Gap** |
| Unison/octave/fifth/fourth rotation | No explicit selectable stack/transition strategy | **Gap** |
| Long held-note lifecycle | tracked `harmonize_note_on/off`, active-note storage | **Available** |
| Register spreading | `OctaveMode::{Spread, BassTrebleSplit, Mirror}` | **Partial; Mirror is unsuitable** |
| Voice-leading continuity | optional `VoiceLeadingProcessor` | **Partial; style rules are not Notre-Dame-specific** |
| Parallel perfect intervals | fourth mode can produce them | **Possible**, but later voice-leading/counterpoint processing may conflict |
| Beat awareness | `BeatPhase`; counterpoint phase and synthetic counter | **Available plumbing** |
| Measured clausula rhythm | HarmonyEngine produces notes reactively, not autonomous modal ordines | **Gap at engine level** |
| Phrase detection/cadence state | no chant-tone duration/phrase-rest state machine in audited paths | **Gap** |
| Section switching | no Purum/Discant/Triplum state in supplied engine | **Gap** |
| Global sonority checks | harmonies are generated as outward chains | **Gap** |
| Historical tuning/ficta | 12-TET MIDI scale and generic modal interchange | **Gap** |

### 16.2 Explicit interval-stack feasibility

`HarmonyEngine::harmonize()` chains each new harmony from the preceding generated note. In `DiatonicFourths`, three voices can therefore become a **stack of diatonic fourths**, not a declarative set of intervals against the tenor. This cannot guarantee requested tenor-relative structures such as:

```text
[T, T+P5, T+P8]
[T, T+P4, T+P8]
```

Nor can it select a different interval stack at attack, continuation, and cadence. Chaining also does not validate relationships between nonadjacent voices. The preset catalog’s stated requirement—**explicit interval stacks**—is therefore confirmed by code inspection.

Minimum required representation:

```text
intervals relative to anchor/tenor, per temporal state
```

not:

```text
apply the same interval recursively to the previous voice
```

No new general-purpose “medieval engine” is justified until that smaller primitive exists.

### 16.3 Existing modes that should not be substituted

- `StrictCounterpoint`: explicitly prefers later species-style behavior and avoids parallel fifths/octaves; wrong baseline.
- `DiatonicThirds`: stacks thirds into seventh-chord-like structures; wrong.
- `RandomBelowNoSeconds`: may output thirds through sevenths without phrase direction; wrong.
- `FunctionalHarmony` / `BachChorale`: wrong tonal and voice-leading model.
- `OctaveMode::Mirror`: duplicates every harmony at ±octaves and exceeds bounded historical texture.

### 16.4 Companion / PatternLane mapping

The supplied source audit establishes beat-phase plumbing in `HarmonyEngine` but did not include Companion or PatternLane implementations. Therefore only the following capability claims are safe:

- A beat-synchronized PatternLane could plausibly host a repeated long–short or short–long **discant approximation** if it supports:
  - explicit per-step duration;
  - phrase-bounded reset;
  - rests;
  - note-off cleanup;
  - intervals relative to the held tenor;
  - transport stop behavior.
- A single pattern lane cannot by itself produce independent triplum/quadruplum unless lanes have separate rhythmic patterns, bounded registers, synchronized cadence points, and all-voice sonority validation.
- Organum purum should not be forced into PatternLane quantization unless the lane supports unequal/free gesture timing and release-triggered cadences.

**Named code gap:** `NotreDameIntervalStack` or equivalent data-level tenor-relative interval selection.  
**Named temporal gap:** `Purum → Discant → Cadence` phrase/section state.  
**Named lane gap:** phrase-bounded rhythmic-mode ordines with reset.  
**Named polyphonic gap:** independent multi-lane upper voices with global sonority checks.  
**Named modal gap:** medieval chant-mode/ficta behavior beyond a seven-note modern mode.  
**Named articulation gap:** generated melismatic events during one sustained input note.

---

## 17. Smallest honest preset recommendation

### Operational scope now

Implement only a **Cloister Organum — Duplum approximation**:

- clean monophonic input interpreted as slow chant tenor;
- two voices total;
- input in lowest voice position;
- user-selected diatonic mode;
- no modal interchange;
- long notes and explicit rests;
- added voice constrained to an explicitly selected fourth, fifth, or octave relationship;
- phrase attack/cadence biased to fifth or octave;
- no `StrictCounterpoint`, functional harmony, or Mirror mode.

However, current `HarmonyEngine` cannot generate a florid multi-note duplum from one sustained tenor note. Without a Companion lane or hold-time gesture generator, the actual result remains **punctum-against-punctum open-interval harmonization**, not organum purum.

### Availability decision

**`needs_more_capability`**

The title may be previewed only with explicit approximation copy such as:

> “Open-interval chant harmonization inspired by Notre-Dame organum; does not reproduce its florid duplum or measured clausulae.”

Do not advertise triplum/quadruplum until independent lanes and global sonority validation exist.

---

## 18. Confidence and competing interpretations

| Claim | Confidence | Qualification |
|---|---|---|
| Organum purum has sustained tenor and florid duplum | High | Core repertorial definition |
| Discant/clausula has both voices measured | High | Rhythm can still vary by source and transcription |
| Pérotin-style added voices move at comparable rates above slow tenor | High | Exact local modal realization varies |
| Purum should not receive one rigid rhythmic mode | Medium-high | Some editors hear modal implications in ligatures/c copula-like passages |
| Structural consonance governs important rhythmic meetings | High | Exact consonance taxonomy and transcription remain debated |
| Medieval modality can be represented by modern Dorian/etc. | Low as equivalence; medium as approximation | Must be disclosed as approximation |
| Pythagorean tuning is the exact required tuning | Low | Plausible option, not uniquely prescribed |
| Every cadence must end at octave/unison | Medium | Strong operational simplification, not a universal corpus law |
| Léonin personally composed all attributed duplum | Low–medium | Anonymous IV is retrospective |
| Pérotin alone authored all associated tripla/quadrupla | Low–medium | Repertorial attribution remains mediated by later testimony |

### Principal scholarly disagreement

The greatest implementation-sensitive disagreement concerns **organum-purum rhythm**. A rigidly modal realization is not defensible as the sole answer; neither is shapeless note-by-note freedom. The safest operational interpretation is flexible, grouped melody whose timing responds to ligature-like gesture, consonance, breath, and tenor articulation.

---

## Sources

### Kept

- Ernest H. Sanders, [“Consonance and Rhythm in the Organum of the 12th and 13th Centuries”](https://doi.org/10.2307/831113) — foundational account of consonant coordination and rhythmic weight.
- Jeremy Yudkin, [“The Rhythm of Organum Purum”](https://doi.org/10.2307/763685) — central corrective against blanket modal transcription.
- Asher V. Yampolsky, [*Melodic Mode in Notre Dame Organum Duplum*](https://eprints.soton.ac.uk/482281/) — corpus-based evidence for modal and dronal organization.
- Catherine A. Bradley, [*Creating Clausulae at Notre-Dame-de-Paris*](https://www.repository.cam.ac.uk/items/09fe45cf-e487-467e-aeea-575d40f0fb28) — detailed account of tenor design, recurring upper-voice techniques, and measured clausula composition.
- Penelope Turner, [“Notre Dame Organum Duplum: What Does a Performer Need?”](https://www.musicandpractice.org/volume-1/notre-dame-organum-duplum-modern-edition/) — compares manuscript/editorial rhythm and explains responsive tenor performance.
- Richard Taruskin, [“Organum cum alio”](https://www.oxfordwesternmusic.com/view/Volume1/actrade-9780195384819-div1-006005.xml) — clear distinction between duplum and Pérotin-generation multi-upper-voice practice.
- Catherine A. Bradley, [“Who ‘Made’ the Magnus Liber?”](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0261127901001061) — attribution and compilation caution.
- University of Basel, [“Rhythmic patterns—how to recognise a mode”](https://tales.nmc.unibas.ch/en/from-ink-to-sound-32/coordination-in-rhythm-modal-notation-189/rhythmic-patterns-how-to-recognise-a-mode-957) — institutional explanation of six rhythmic modes and phrase-level ligature patterns.
- Rebecca A. Baltzer, [“Notre Dame,” *The Cambridge History of Medieval Music*](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/cambridge-history-of-medieval-music/notre-dame/94C93F0FE9B8B2690D8329693A9FCA83) — authoritative repertorial overview and bibliography.
- Mary E. Wolinski, [“Organum at Notre-Dame in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries: rhetoric in words and music”](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0961137106000349) — broader account of tripla/quadrupla elaboration and liturgical-rhetorical context.

### Dropped

- Wikipedia summaries — useful discovery aids but unnecessary where scholarship or primary-treatise translations were available.
- Scribd uploads and personal blogs — unclear provenance or secondary teaching material.
- Modern “cathedral sound” explainers — often conflate acoustics, instrumentation, and later performance traditions.
- Generic early-organum rules predating the Notre-Dame repertory — risk importing ninth- through eleventh-century parallel-organum practice into the selected corpus.

---

## Gaps

1. Exact interval-frequency statistics by texture and manuscript were not available in the accessible source abstracts; a score-based W1/F/W2 sample should validate numerical weights before implementation.
2. Exact cadence profiles for selected *Viderunt*/*Sederunt* passages require consultation of the modern critical edition or manuscript facsimiles.
3. PatternLane and Companion source files were not among the supplied audit files, so their phrase reset, relative-pitch, autonomous-note, and multi-lane synchronization behavior must be verified before claiming support.
4. Historical tuning, ensemble size, tempo, ficta, and organum-purum rhythm remain legitimate performance variables rather than preset-certifiable facts.

# Research: Preset 01 — Cloister Organum  
## Music theory and temporal behavior

## Summary

A defensible Notre-Dame preset must not reduce Léonin and Pérotin to parallel fourths. The repertory alternates three materially different behaviors: **organum purum** (a freely flowing duplum over a sustained chant tone), **discant/clausula** (both voices measured in rhythmic modes), and **triplum/quadruplum** (two or three rhythmically coordinated upper voices over a much slower chant tenor). The smallest honest Contrapunk implementation is therefore a bounded **two-voice, chant-tenor organum-purum approximation** using modal pitch material, long input holds, predominantly perfect-consonance arrivals, and phrase rests; explicit interval-stack selection and sectional rhythmic-state switching remain named gaps.

---

## 1. Scope and corpus

### Selected repertory

This report draws its rules from:

- two-voice *Magnus liber organi* repertory associated by the later testimony of Anonymous IV with **Léonin**, especially organa dupla such as *Viderunt omnes* and the broader W1/F/W2 transmitted corpus;
- the Notre-Dame repertory of **two-part discant clausulae**, including substitute clausula practice;
- the three- and four-voice repertory associated with **Pérotin**, especially *Viderunt omnes* and *Sederunt principes*, plus the larger tripla/quadrupla practice.

The repertory survives chiefly in the manuscript complexes commonly called W1, F, and W2. The modern *Magnus Liber Organi* edition itself reflects materially different editorial decisions about the underdetermined rhythm of sustained-tenor passages. [Turner, “Notre Dame Organum Duplum”](https://www.musicandpractice.org/volume-1/notre-dame-organum-duplum-modern-edition/)

### Attribution caution

Anonymous IV’s account linking Léonin with the *Magnus liber* and Pérotin with revisions and large-scale tripla/quadrupla was written decades later. “Léonin style” and “Pérotin style” are useful repertorial labels, not secure modern authorship metadata. Scholarship also emphasizes compilation, oral practice, substitution, and reuse rather than a fixed authored work in the modern sense. [Bradley, “Who ‘Made’ the Magnus Liber?”](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0261127901001061)

**Preset scope:** late-twelfth-/early-thirteenth-century Parisian liturgical organum, with the operational baseline centered on **organum duplum/purum**, not a claim to reproduce every Notre-Dame texture.

**Confidence:** High for the three-way stylistic distinction; medium for individual attributions.

---

## 2. Three practices that must remain separate

| Practice | Tenor behavior | Added-voice behavior | Rhythmic organization | Operational identity |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Organum purum / organum per se** | One chant pitch sustained for a long span | One florid duplum, usually above it | Rhythm underdetermined/free; ligatures shape gestures without proving one continuous rhythmic mode | Drone-like span, but with responsive intervallic articulation |
| **Discant / clausula** | Chant melisma segmented into repeated/measured notes | Duplum rhythmically active against tenor | Modal, measurable rhythm; phrases/ordines bounded by rests | Propulsive two-part rhythmic counterpoint |
| **Organum triplum/quadruplum / cum alio** | Very slow chant foundation | Two or three upper voices moving at broadly comparable rates | Upper voices coordinated through modal rhythmic organization | Layered upper-voice polyphony, not parallel interval duplication |

Organum purum’s free rhythm remains disputed in detail, but modern performers and editors broadly distinguish it from the more securely measurable discant passages. Turner warns that forcing sustained-tenor passages into a fixed “lilting” modal rhythm destroys their flexibility. [Turner](https://www.musicandpractice.org/volume-1/notre-dame-organum-duplum-modern-edition/); [Yudkin, “The Rhythm of Organum Purum”](https://doi.org/10.2307/763685)

Pérotin-generation “organum cum alio” adds voices that move at the duplum’s rate rather than at the tenor’s rate; consequently, the added voices are in discant with one another even while all unfold above the slow chant. [Taruskin, “Organum cum alio”](https://www.oxfordwesternmusic.com/view/Volume1/actrade-9780195384819-div1-006005.xml)

**Confidence:** High.

---

## 3. Tonal center, modality, chromaticism, and tuning

### 3.1 Tonal organization

1. The lowest voice is a pre-existing chant, not a generated functional bass.
2. Pitch organization derives from medieval chant modality, recurrent melodic outlines, finals, reciting/focal pitches, and the locally sustained tenor pitch.
3. The current tenor pitch creates a temporary **dronal center**, while the work’s chant mode supplies the larger pitch hierarchy.
4. A modern “key + scale” is only an approximation: mode cannot be inferred reliably from the final alone, and individual chants may change local orientation.

Yampolsky’s corpus analysis argues that organum-purum melodic material is primarily mode-dependent, while also finding a strong local dronal hearing and one analytical dimension better explained by consonance. [Yampolsky, *Melodic Mode in Notre Dame Organum Duplum*](https://eprints.soton.ac.uk/482281/)

### 3.2 Operational rule

- Require a user-selected chant final/mode approximation.
- Keep the pitch collection diatonic by default.
- Treat the held input as the **local tenor reference**, not automatically as a new tonic on every note.
- Do not introduce functional dominant–tonic progressions, major/minor chord syntax, blues chromaticism, or automatic modal interchange.
- Musica ficta and B-flat/B-natural choices are source- and context-dependent; they should not be randomized by a preset.

### 3.3 Tuning

The notation does not prescribe a single modern tuning standard. Pythagorean-leaning intonation is historically plausible for perfect intervals, but exact pitch, temperament, ensemble composition, and ficta remain performance decisions. The preset should prioritize pure-sounding unisons, fifths, fourths, and octaves if microtuning ever becomes available, but must not advertise an exact historical temperament.

**Confidence:**  
- Modal/dronal organization: High.  
- Exact ficta per generic preset: Low.  
- Pythagorean tuning as one defensible realization: Medium.

**Competing interpretation:** Mode-centered and consonance-centered analyses are not mutually exclusive; modal melodic design governs the line while consonance governs important vertical meetings.
